column3: It names David as God's servant and repeatedly returning one, directly establishing the pattern extended to Solomon.
Zechariah's prayer for a good offspring provides a related instance of a child sought as divine gift.
The immediate continuation tests Solomon and records his return, directly unfolding the focus's final description.
Its good place of return gives the fulfilled outcome corresponding to Solomon's repeated return to God.
Job is called an excellent servant and repeatedly returning one in the same formula used for Solomon.
Solomon's good place of return completes the same David-Solomon narrative with the outcome of right return.
It pairs Solomon with David and specifies Solomon's God-given understanding, concretizing the bestowed son.
The refusal of a rival worship pattern only broadly relates to the focus's description of a servant.
The birds gathered with David are each described as returning to God, extending David's devotional setting.
The return-place term supplies a punitive contrast to the excellent servant's return to God.
Isaac and Jacob are likewise bestowed as offspring, paralleling Solomon's status as a divine gift.
Exclusive worship of God supplies the defining allegiance implicit in calling Solomon an excellent servant.
Job's restored family is a divine gift, but it does not clarify Solomon's filial gift or return.
Abraham thanks God for sons given in old age, framing offspring as gift rather than possession.
Aaron's being given to Moses shows divine gift operating through family and prophetic support.
Abraham's request for a righteous child parallels the focus's presentation of Solomon as a given son.
Solomon's letter begins in God's name, offering a direct instance of his God-centered rule.
Solomon asks the Giver for a kingdom after seeking forgiveness, immediately developing gift and return in the same account.
God's gift of mercy and enduring honor to Abraham's family broadly parallels bestowed familial favor.
Turning to God after rejecting false worship links devoted servanthood with the return named in the focus.
Isaac and Jacob are bestowed within a lineage that carries prophecy, a wider parallel to David's gifted son.
It promises reward to every repeatedly returning keeper, clarifying the positive horizon of Solomon's description.
God's being the excellent protector loosely echoes the praise term, without the servant or return context.
The announced gift of a pure son directly supports reading Solomon's sonship as bestowed rather than owned.
The affirmative response has no substantive connection beyond a shared surface token.
God's justice toward servants gives only a general background for the servant designation in the focus.
Solomon rejects a diplomatic gift by crediting God's gift as better, enacting dependence rather than possession.
The evil place of return for transgressors contrasts with the good return associated with faithful servants.
Under Solomon's rule the queen acknowledges her wrong and submits to God, showing his rule oriented beyond himself.
The purified servants are protected from satanic diversion, a related model of undivided servanthood.
The excellent reward for workers has only a broad lexical relation to calling Solomon excellent.
Honored servants are distinguished from divine offspring, supporting the focus's insistence that even gifted figures are servants.
Its excellent reward and resting place do not address the focus's gifted son or repeated return.
The good return promised to the God-conscious situates Solomon's return in the same surah's final horizon.
Non-participation in others' worship is only a general counterpart to being God's servant.
The repeated separation of worship communities offers a limited background for exclusive servanthood.
Thankfulness for provision and worship of God are broadly related but do not illuminate Solomon specifically.
Zechariah is introduced as God's servant receiving mercy, a parallel servant-and-gift setting.
It explicitly joins worship of God, calling to Him, and returning to Him, clarifying the focus's devotional direction.
The denial of injustice toward servants gives only general context for God's relation to servants.
It merely mentions what people worship, without explaining Solomon's excellent service.
Paradise inherited by God-conscious servants gives a related destination for the faithful servant relation.
David is joined by mountains and birds commanded to return in praise, directly framing the devotional household of the focus.
God is named the Bestower in the same surah, grounding Solomon's status as a bestowed gift.
It explicitly lists David and Solomon within a divinely bestowed and guided prophetic lineage.
Zechariah's request for an heir frames a successor as an unearned gift from God.
It directly pairs David and Solomon in judgment, showing the son acting alongside his father.
David's forgiveness and good return provide the father's adjacent pattern of restoration and return.
Solomon inherits David and openly recognizes his exceptional endowment as manifest divine favor.
Universal coming to the Merciful as servants reinforces that even honored sons remain God's servants.
Yahya's being bestowed after prayer is another clear instance of offspring as divine gift.
God's judgment among His servants affirms the sole authority before which the servant stands.
David's mountains are made to praise with him, supplying immediate devotional context for the Davidic household.
The coming promise to God's servants gives a positive future horizon for faithful service.
The question about angels supplies no meaningful connection to Solomon's gift or service.
After leaving false worship, Abraham receives gifted offspring and prophecy, joining exclusive service and gift.
Jesus is both a servant and one favored by God, closely clarifying how extraordinary favor does not cancel servanthood.
It rejects treating God's servants as portions of Him, reinforcing the distinction between servant and divine status.
God's final inheritance is only a distant background to the focus's bestowed son.
The command to prostrate and worship gives the basic allegiance expressed in Solomon's excellent servanthood.
Noah is identified as one of God's believing servants, providing a related exemplary servant designation.
Noah's call to worship God alone supplies the exclusive devotion underlying faithful service.
Pharaoh's claim of a favor through Israel's enslavement contrasts coercive ownership with God's honored servanthood.
It explicitly invites each person to take a path of return to his Lord, directly clarifying awwab's direction.
The ruler's affirmative answer and offer of closeness do not illuminate the focus.
A messenger calls his people to worship God alone, a general articulation of servant allegiance.
The affirmative reward promise has no substantive relation to Solomon's gift or return.
God's servants pray for forgiveness and mercy, showing a communal posture of dependence before God.
It presents Solomon leading an army, a narrative context that contrasts his authority with the focus's servant identity.
The assured return to God gives the final, compulsory horizon against which voluntary repeated return is meaningful.
The prayer seeks mercy from the Bestower after guidance, linking divine gift with sustained right direction.
The prayer for spouses and offspring as gifts offers a familial parallel to Solomon's bestowed sonship.
It explicitly clears Solomon of disbelief and locates his kingdom outside the corrupt practices attributed to it.
Moses describes judgment and messengerhood as gifts from his Lord, paralleling bestowed authority and vocation.
Calling the Quran a reminder does not clarify Solomon's gift, service, or return.
Satan's claim of a share among God's servants is a remote contrast to faithful service.
The affirmative reply about fulfilled promises has no substantive relation to the focus.
God is forgiving toward those who repeatedly return, directly explaining the moral character named of Solomon.
The refusal to worship another object only broadly relates to exclusive service of God.
Divine justice toward servants is general background rather than a link to Solomon's particular praise.
Knowledgeable servants' fear of God supplies a related quality of exemplary service.
God addresses even sinful people as His servants and opens forgiveness, a restorative context for returning to Him.
Solomon attributes favor to God, asks to be grateful and righteous, and seeks entry among God's righteous servants.
God's servant stands to call upon Him, directly illustrating active devoted service.
Thanking God for His favor while worshiping Him joins gift, gratitude, and service.
God's granting of children by His will directly reinforces Solomon's status as a bestowed son.
Worldly desire for sons is contrasted with the better return with God, reframing offspring beyond possession.
Supposed deities are reduced to servants like their callers, reinforcing creaturely servanthood over false elevation.
David recognizes the test, seeks forgiveness, prostrates, and returns, directly supplying the father's return pattern.
Jesus identifies first as God's servant before his granted book and prophecy, clarifying honor within servanthood.
God's excellent response to Noah's call offers only a distant lexical parallel to excellent service.
Praise and seeking forgiveness because God is ever accepting of return closely support a life of return to Him.
The warning about Satan as an enemy lacks a direct link to Solomon's gift or service.
The demand for pure religion to God contrasts mediated worship and clarifies exclusive servant allegiance.
The command concerning an orphan has no substantive connection to the focus.
The description of disbelievers does not clarify Solomon's gift, service, or return.
The accusation of obvious magic has no meaningful connection to the focus.
The account of testing and divine command gives only remote background to a tested prophetic household.
Rain reaching some of God's servants is a general instance of divine beneficence, not Solomon's bestowed sonship.
Retribution according to deeds gives only a broad moral backdrop to exemplary service.
God gives David kingship and wisdom, supplying the father’s divinely granted authority from which Solomon’s succession is later shown.
Solomon is explicitly named among the prophets receiving revelation, directly confirming his bestowed prophetic vocation.
David’s receipt of the Psalms supplies a related divine gift within the father’s prophetic household.
The wind is subjected to Solomon by God, directly showing exceptional authority held under divine bestowal.
The devils’ labor for Solomon occurs only under God’s preserving authority, clarifying his rule as granted rather than autonomous.
David and Solomon receive knowledge and answer with praise, directly framing their inherited prophetic house by gratitude to God.
Solomon’s assembled forces display royal power while the focus defines its bearer first as God’s servant.
Solomon’s inspection of the birds gives narrative context for his exercised authority and responsible rule.
Solomon’s stated discipline of the hoopoe gives further context for the judgment exercised within his granted kingdom.
The hoopoe’s report initiates the episode in which Solomon’s authority is directed toward knowledge and invitation to God.
The report of the queen’s great throne sets the political setting that Solomon’s God-centered rule will confront.
The queen’s people worship the sun, supplying the false devotion answered by Solomon’s summons to God.
The call to worship God alone clarifies the devotion toward which Solomon’s letter and rule are directed.
God’s sole lordship and magnificent throne contrast with the queen’s throne and frame Solomon’s authority as subordinate.
Solomon tests the report rather than acting blindly, giving a practical instance of his wise rule.
Solomon’s letter calls its recipients to return with a response, beginning his direct summons under God’s name.
The queen identifies Solomon’s letter as noble, preparing the explicit God-centered wording preserved in the next verse.
Solomon’s letter commands that they not exalt themselves and that they come submitting to God, directly embodying devoted rule.
The queen seeks counsel about Solomon’s summons, showing its public and political force.
Her council foregrounds military strength, the worldly power that Solomon’s message redirects toward submission to God.
The queen’s warning about kings gives a countermodel against which Solomon’s servant identity qualifies royal power.
The proposed gift provides the immediate setup for Solomon’s refusal to treat divine favor as exchangeable wealth.
Solomon rejects the queen’s position of resistance and directs the encounter toward submission rather than reciprocal patronage.
Solomon asks which servant will bring the throne, displaying authority exercised through a gathered court under God.
The ifrit’s offer demonstrates the extraordinary capacities available within Solomon’s divinely ordered kingdom.
Solomon calls the throne’s arrival a favor from his Lord and a test of gratitude, directly enacting gifted power and servanthood.
Solomon tests the queen’s recognition through her altered throne, continuing his measured exercise of authority.
The queen’s recognition of prior guidance advances the narrative of insight and submission shaped by Solomon’s encounter.
Her prior worship had obstructed her, providing the direct religious obstacle to the submission reached in the following verse.
David is commanded to make armor and act righteously, supplying a related model of gifted skill governed by service.
The wind and jinn are subjected to Solomon by God, directly portraying the bestowed dominion subsequent verses develop.
Solomon’s workers are told to act in gratitude, directly joining extraordinary provision to accountable service.
The immediate scene of Solomon’s prized horses begins the narrative that tests how royal goods relate to remembrance of God.
Solomon explicitly connects his love of fine horses with remembrance of his Lord, directly displaying the focus’s returning devotion.
Solomon’s response to the horses completes the immediate scene of his disciplined relation to royal resources.
God subjects the wind to Solomon at his command, directly presenting his authority as a divine grant.
The devils are subjected to Solomon as builders and divers, extending the specific gifts of his God-given kingdom.
Other devils are bound together, further specifying the controlled forces within Solomon’s bestowed rule.
God explicitly calls the kingdom His gift and permits Solomon to give or withhold, directly interpreting the focus’s statement that Solomon was bestowed.
David’s appointment to judge with truth supplies the father’s accountable rule that contextualizes Solomon’s inherited kingship.
